chemicals.concentration_notes: or potency: The severity depends on the dose; high doses result in acute, severe liver damage and sudden death, while prolonged low-dose exposure causes reduced growth rates and liver enlargement.
chemicals.description: Peanuts are highly susceptible to becoming damp and developing Aspergillus mold, which produces aflatoxins14. If an animal ingests moldy peanuts, it causes aflatoxicosis. This disrupts normal cellular function, leading to severe liver damage, ruptured blood vessels (internal bleeding), and jaundice.
chemicals.name: Aflatoxins (Mold Contamination)

chemicals.concentration_notes: or potency: Allergic reactions are not strictly dose-dependent but rely on the individual animal's specific immune sensitivity.
chemicals.description: The specific proteins in peanuts can trigger a severe immune system overreaction. The sources note that peanuts can specifically cause a "deadly allergic reaction" in pets3. Any notes on concentration or potency: Allergic reactions are not strictly dose-dependent but rely on the individual animal's specific immune sensitivity.
chemicals.name: Peanut Allergens

chemicals.concentration_notes: or potency: Xylitol is extremely potent; in dogs, doses as low as 100 mg/kg cause severe hypoglycemia, and doses over 500 mg/kg cause liver failure.
chemicals.description: Many commercial peanut butters use xylitol as an artificial, sugar-free sweetener. In dogs, xylitol triggers a massive insulin release causing life-threatening hypoglycemia and possible liver failure. Cats, however, are not affected: the Merck Veterinary Manual states cats are not at risk for hypoglycemia or liver injury from xylitol, and the ASPCA reports no known xylitol toxicity in cats. It is still prudent to keep xylitol products away from cats.
chemicals.name: Xylitol (Found in Peanut Butter)

chemicals.concentration_notes: or potency: The sources note that large amounts of salt can be fatal to pets1516. Treats containing these ingredients should make up no more than 10% of a pet's daily caloric intake, though peanuts are advised against entirely.
chemicals.description: Peanuts are naturally very high in oils and fats, and human peanut snacks are frequently seasoned with high amounts of salt4. A cat's digestive system cannot easily process dense plant fats, which leads to severe indigestion, diarrhea, and the potential to trigger pancreatitis (a painful inflammation of the pancreas)1314.
chemicals.name: High Fats and Added Salt (Processed Peanuts)

description:
Plain, unsalted peanuts do not contain any specific poisons that are toxic to cats, but they are still not a good snack choice. Peanuts are very high in fat, and cats have a hard time digesting them. Eating too much fat can lead to pancreatitis, which is a painful and potentially life-threatening swelling of the pancreas.

Another hidden danger with peanuts is mold. Peanuts can easily grow a type of mold that produces aflatoxins, which can cause severe liver damage if eaten. Additionally, most peanuts sold in stores are roasted with a lot of salt or artificial flavorings, which are harmful to a cat's kidneys. Peanut butter is also very high in fat and salt. Some brands contain xylitol, a sweetener that is dangerous to dogs; unlike in dogs, xylitol is not a documented poison for cats, but it is still best avoided.

While a single plain peanut probably will not hurt your cat, regular feeding can cause long-term health issues. Keep salted peanuts and peanut butter away from your cat. If your cat eats moldy peanuts, contact a veterinarian right away.
emergencyNote: Because peanuts do not contain a specific inherent chemical poison
name: Peanuts
safetyNotes: Not acutely toxic: plain peanuts do not contain cat-specific toxins
Fat risk: very high fat content; regular feeding can cause pancreatitis (painful, potentially fatal pancreatic inflammation)
Aflatoxin risk: mouldy or improperly stored peanuts may contain aflatoxins, which cause liver damage
Salted, flavoured, or roasted peanuts: high sodium and artificial seasonings are harmful to cats

Peanut butter: high in fat and often excessive salt — the relevant cat risks; xylitol in some brands is a serious dog hazard but is not documented to harm cats (Merck/ASPCA); a tiny taste of plain peanut butter is unlikely to cause harm

symptoms.name: Aflatoxicosis (From Moldy Peanuts)
symptoms.notes: Peanuts are susceptible to growing Aspergillus fungi, which produce toxic aflatoxins1. Ingestion of these moldy peanuts results in severe liver damage and the rupturing of blood vessels.
symptoms.onset: Acute (shortly after a large dose) or chronic (developing progressively over time with low-dose expo

symptoms.name: Xylitol (From Peanut Butter) — Dog Hazard, Not a Cat Hazard
symptoms.notes: Many peanut butters are sweetened with xylitol. This is a serious, sometimes fatal poison for dogs, but it is not a documented hazard for cats: the Merck Veterinary Manual states that cats are not at risk for hypoglycemia or liver injury from xylitol, and the ASPCA reports no known xylitol toxicity in cats. Xylitol-sweetened peanut butter is still best kept away from cats as a precaution.

symptoms.name: Sodium Ion Poisoning (From Salted Peanuts)
symptoms.notes: Human peanut snacks are frequently heavily seasoned with salt, which unnecessarily increases the metabolic burden on a cat's kidneys.
symptoms.onset: Within minutes to hours of ingestion

symptoms.name: Indigestion and Pancreatitis (From High Fat Content)
symptoms.notes: Peanuts are rich in oils and have a hard physical texture that easily leads to indigestion and diarrhea in cats4. Furthermore, consuming high-fat foods can trigger pancreatitis, a painful and potentially life-threatening inflammation of the pancreas.
symptoms.onset: Within a few hours (for standard indigestion) or progressively over days (for pancreatitis)

symptoms.name: Allergic Reaction (Rare)
symptoms.notes: Food-triggered allergic reactions, including rare anaphylaxis, are possible in cats, but no authoritative veterinary source documents peanut-specific fatal allergic reactions in cats. Treat this as a rare, unconfirmed risk rather than an expected outcome.

treatments.name: Because peanuts do not contain a specific inherent chemical poison

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the ingestion is caught very early (within a couple of hours) and the cat has not yet developed symptoms, the veterinarian may administer a specific injection to induce vomiting (emesis) to empty the stomach and minimize absorption.
treatments.name: Rapid Hypoglycemia Management & Decontamination (If Xylitol-sweetened peanut butter was ingested)
treatments.notes: Pet owners must never attempt to induce vomiting in cats at home, as there are no safe methods to do so without professional supervision.

treatments.description: of the procedure: The veterinarian will measure the cat's serum sodium and electrolyte levels and administer specific IV fluids to help dilute the sodium in the blood. The goal is to slowly return the animal to a normal water and electrolyte balance over a period of 2 to 3 days.
treatments.name: Controlled Sodium Correction (If heavily salted peanuts were ingested)
treatments.notes: It is critical that the veterinarian lowers the sodium concentration slowly. If fluids are given too rapidly, it increases the osmotic gradient between the blood and the brain, drawing water into the brain cells and causing severe, potentially fatal cerebral edema (brain swelling)

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the cat experiences a severe immune overreaction, the vet will provide immediate life-saving stabilization (such as airway support, oxygen, and emergency medications) to counteract the systemic allergic response.
treatments.name: Emergency Anaphylaxis Response (If an allergic reaction occurs)
treatments.notes: Peanuts have been specifically identified as a food capable of triggering a "deadly allergic reaction" in pets.

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the high fat in the peanuts triggers pancreatitis, the cat will be hospitalized and given IV fluids to correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities10. The vet will administer anti-nausea medications (such as maropitant) and prescribe pain relief (such as the opioid buprenorphine).
treatments.name: Intensive Medical Management for Pancreatitis (If triggered by high fat content)
treatments.notes: Early nutritional support is critical in feline pancreatitis to prevent prolonged anorexia, which can quickly lead to a secondary, life-threatening liver condition known as hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver)
